title: The 134-Year Wait: Inside the Green Card Crisis Crushing Indian Dreams in America
excerpt: With 1.1 million Indians trapped in a backlog that defies logic, the employment-based immigration system has become a generational burden for the diaspora
body:
Somewhere in the sprawling bureaucratic apparatus of US immigration, there is a queue. In that queue, more than 1.1 million Indian nationals are waiting for an employment-based green card—the document that would, after years of paying taxes, raising families, and building careers in America, finally grant them the right to call the country home. The wait, for many, will outlast their working lives. By some estimates, it could stretch to 134 years.

## A System Designed for Another Era

The crisis is structural. Under US immigration law, no single country can receive more than 7% of the roughly 140,000 employment-based green cards issued annually. This per-country cap, enshrined in Section 202 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, was designed in an era when immigration patterns were more evenly distributed. It was never built to accommodate a world in which Indian nationals, overwhelmingly employed in technology, healthcare, and engineering, would come to dominate demand for skilled-worker visas.

The result is a backlog of staggering proportions. The total employment-based green card backlog now exceeds 1.8 million cases, with India accounting for more than 60% of the total. For Indian applicants in the EB-2 category—the most common pathway for professionals with advanced degrees—the State Department's Visa Bulletin shows a "final action date" stuck at July 2013. In practical terms, this means that an Indian professional who filed their green card application in 2013 is only now becoming eligible for processing. Those filing today face waits of 10 to 15 years or more.

## Living in Limbo

The human cost of this bureaucratic gridlock is immense and largely invisible to the American public. Indian professionals on H-1B visas—the temporary work permit that most use while awaiting a green card—live in a state of perpetual precarity. They cannot freely change employers without jeopardising their place in the queue. Their spouses, many of whom hold advanced degrees of their own, have only recently gained the right to work, and even that remains subject to policy reversals. Their children, raised as Americans in every meaningful sense, face the prospect of "ageing out" of their parents' application at 21, potentially losing their immigration status altogether.

A recent analysis by the Cato Institute found that more than 134,000 children of Indian green card applicants are at risk of ageing out before their parents' cases are resolved. For these families, the American Dream has become an exercise in indefinite patience, punctuated by anxiety.

## Legislative Deadlock

Efforts to fix the system have repeatedly stalled in Congress. The EAGLE Act, which would eliminate per-country caps and establish a first-come, first-served system, has drawn bipartisan support in some quarters but faces opposition from lawmakers who argue it would disadvantage applicants from smaller countries. The bill's prospects in 2026 remain dim, with immigration legislation of any kind struggling to gain traction in a polarised Congress.

In the absence of congressional action, some Indian professionals are turning to alternative pathways. EB-1A petitions, reserved for individuals of "extraordinary ability," have seen a surge in applications from Indian nationals, though approval rates remain uneven. Others are exploring the EB-5 investor visa, which offers faster processing in exchange for a substantial financial commitment—typically $800,000 or more.

## The Diaspora Calculus

Increasingly, Indian professionals are asking a question that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago: is the wait worth it? Canada's Express Entry system offers permanent residency in six to twelve months. Germany's new Opportunity Card provides a fast track for skilled workers. Australia and the United Kingdom have revamped their points-based systems to attract precisely the sort of talent that America is forcing to wait in line.

The data suggests that some are voting with their feet. Applications from Indian nationals to Canadian immigration programmes have surged over the past three years, and India is now the single largest source country for Canada's permanent residents. For the United States, the risk is not merely humanitarian but economic: a generation of engineers, doctors, and entrepreneurs, trained and employed on American soil, may simply choose to build their futures elsewhere.

## What Comes Next

The May 2026 Visa Bulletin brought no relief. USCIS confirmed it will use the Final Action Dates chart for EB-3 India, with an effective cut-off date of November 15, 2013—a marginal movement that offers little comfort to the hundreds of thousands still waiting. Until Congress acts, the green card backlog will continue to grow, a monument to the gap between America's demand for skilled labour and its willingness to welcome those who provide it.
